item.title: Africa’s AI & Enterprise Revolution Will Be Built on Infrastructure That Doesn’t Fail
item.dc:creator: Samuel
item.content:encoded:
There’s no shortage of excitement around Africa’s digital future. From AI-driven solutions to IoT deployments and ambitious enterprise digital transformation projects in Africa, everyone’s eyes are on the prize. But there’s something missing in most of these conversations: the infrastructure question.

It’s easy to get swept up in possibilities—but none of it happens without infrastructure capable of carrying the weight.

AI & Enterprise Digital Transformation Needs More Than Hype

Artificial intelligence is redefining industries—from agriculture to finance to logistics. The same applies to enterprise technologies like cloud computing, ERP systems, and connected devices. But behind every exciting application lies a less glamorous truth: these innovations are only as strong as the infrastructure supporting them.

AI models require enormous compute power, consistent power supply, low-latency connectivity, and stable storage. Similarly, enterprise systems depend on constant uptime, secure environments, and fast data flows. If a power fluctuation or network bottleneck interrupts a learning model or critical business service, the consequences can be immediate and severe.

As demand scales, the risk of failure rises—unless the infrastructure is purpose-built and future-ready.

The Current Reality in Africa

Across Africa, digital innovation is happening fast—but the digital infrastructure in Ghana and across Africa often struggles to keep up. Many regions still grapple with inconsistent power supply, limited connectivity, and under-resourced data centres. While the private sector is moving quickly, these gaps must be addressed to unlock long-term transformation.

It’s not just about building more—it’s about building smarter. Infrastructure investments should focus on reliability, resilience, and energy efficiency. That includes ensuring better backup systems, robust connectivity pathways, sustainable power solutions, and scalable computing environments.

Quiet Infrastructure, Massive Impact

Infrastructure doesn’t usually make headlines. But it’s the invisible force that underpins every bold technological promise.

When done right, it disappears from view—allowing innovators, telecoms, enterprises, and public institutions to operate smoothly and confidently. When neglected, it becomes a friction point that slows progress.

Africa’s tech future depends on whether this foundation is laid with intention.

Collaboration Over Competition

Meeting the infrastructure needs of a digital Africa isn’t the task of one player. It requires collaboration—between governments, regulators, utilities, telecom providers, and private infrastructure operators. Public-private partnerships will be key in overcoming regional disparities and fast-tracking rollout.

There’s also a growing need to localise investment strategies—adapting infrastructure design and deployment to the realities of each environment. What works in Accra may not work in Tamale or Bujumbura. Understanding local needs and challenges is critical to delivering meaningful, lasting infrastructure.

What Onix Believes

At Onix Data Centres, we view infrastructure not as a commodity, but as a commitment. While we play our part by offering reliable, AI-ready data centres in Ghana, we see ourselves as part of a much larger ecosystem working to strengthen digital infrastructure across the continent.

The future we all imagine—powered by AI, driven by enterprise transformation, and accessible to millions—will only be possible if we get the fundamentals right.

The Long Game

Now is the moment for bold decisions and long-term thinking. Infrastructure might not dazzle on a PowerPoint slide, but it will determine who leads Africa’s digital economy in five, ten, or twenty years.

Africa has the talent, the ideas, and the demand. Let’s ensure it has the digital infrastructure to match—resilient, scalable, and built for the future.

The question isn’t whether enterprise transformation is coming. It’s whether Ghana and Africa are ready for the scale when it does.

Let’s Start the Conversation

If you’re building systems, policies, or partnerships that rely on robust digital infrastructure—let’s talk. Whether you're a telecom provider, enterprise leader, policymaker, or infrastructure partner, the groundwork we lay today will shape tomorrow’s economy.

Reach out to explore how we can work together to build infrastructure that lasts.

item.title: Powering Smart Cities from the Ground Up: The Role of Local Data Centres
item.dc:creator: Samuel
item.content:encoded:
Smart cities sound futuristic—automated transport, intelligent energy use, digital healthcare—but none of it works without robust, local data infrastructure. At the heart of it all? Data centres. These silent powerhouses do the heavy lifting behind the scenes, enabling everything from traffic lights that respond in real time to cloud-powered financial transactions. As Ghana positions itself as a digital leader in West Africa, data centres like Onix are vital to that ambition.

Why Local Data Infrastructure Is Critical

Across much of Africa, digital services still rely on international routing. Data often travels to Europe or the United States before returning to a local device, creating latency, raising security concerns, and adding costs. This dependency delays innovation and introduces risks.

By contrast, a local data centre ecosystem enables faster access to services, improved user experience, and safer data handling. It also ensures data sovereignty: the principle that national data should remain within national borders, governed by local regulations and protected from foreign surveillance.

At Onix, our data remains in Ghana. We support public and private organisations who need fast, secure, and compliant environments to host their most critical systems. In a region that is rapidly digitalising, this is not just an advantage—it's a necessity.

"You can’t build a smart future on imported infrastructure."

The Role of Data Centres in Building Smart Cities

A smart city thrives on data. Whether it’s transport systems adjusting to rush hour congestion, smart electricity grids distributing power efficiently, or emergency services responding based on real-time alerts, everything depends on immediate, accurate data processing.

This is where modern data centres come in:

  • Low-latency performance: Local hosting ensures data doesn’t need to travel across continents.
  • Security and compliance: Critical for sectors like health, education, energy, and finance.
  • Scalability and resilience: Modular infrastructure supports rapid urban expansion and evolving tech demands.
  • Connectivity integration: Seamless connection with multiple carriers, cloud providers, and internet exchanges.

At Onix, our Tier IV facility guarantees 99.995% uptime, providing the resilience needed for applications where downtime isn't an option—like digital hospitals or emergency response systems.

The Smart City Use Cases Already Emerging in Ghana

Ghana is already laying the foundation for smart systems, often powered by local platforms and infrastructure:

1. Digital Payments and Financial Inclusion
  • New platforms are enabling secure, cloud-based financial transactions across both urban and rural areas.
  • These systems improve access to banking services, reduce fraud, and help support micro and small businesses with digital tools.
2. e-Agriculture Platforms
  • Digital tools are being rolled out to support farmers with input tracking, pricing transparency, and supply chain management.
  • Real-time agricultural support and productivity data are improving farming outcomes at scale.
3. Digital Health Services
  • Health institutions across Ghana are increasingly connected, allowing real-time access to patient data, insurance validation, and medical resource planning.
  • These services reduce waiting times and improve healthcare delivery in underserved areas.
4. Smart Utilities
  • Mobile billing, app-based services, and smart meter systems are improving how utilities interact with consumers.
  • These platforms are helping ensure energy efficiency, accurate billing, and reliable service delivery.

These examples are evidence that Ghana is ready for smarter, more efficient systems—and it all depends on resilient, local data infrastructure to scale effectively.. They are active proof that Ghana is ready for smart infrastructure, and it all depends on data centres like Onix to operate seamlessly.

Why Onix is Central to Ghana's Smart Future

At Onix, our infrastructure is purpose-built for the challenges and ambitions of a modern African digital economy. Here's what makes us unique:

Energy Resilience & Sustainability
  • Our solar-powered operations handle 100% of daytime energy needs.
  • Backup systems ensure round-the-clock uptime.
  • This supports national energy goals while keeping operating costs efficient.
Carrier Neutrality & Choice
  • With over 30 network providers and multiple Tier I carriers connected, we offer clients complete flexibility in connectivity.
  • This makes us the optimal hub for any smart application needing fast, low-cost, high-performance internet.
Security and Certification
  • ISO 27001, ISO 9001, and PCI-DSS compliance make us one of the most secure facilities in Africa.
  • Eight-layer physical security, real-time monitoring, and secure access policies protect all customer systems.
Scalable, Modular Design
  • From single racks to entire private cages or dedicated modules, Onix offers space for every business size.
  • As more smart systems come online, customers can scale quickly without changing facilities.
Disaster Recovery & Strategic Placement
  • Our Accra facility is situated outside flood plains, far from industrial risks, and with geostrategic distance from urban congestion—ideal for mission-critical redundancy.
Why the Future Is Local

Africa's digital economy will not grow sustainably if it is built on the infrastructure of other continents. We must build our own. This means:

  • Developing local digital infrastructure that can support everything from e-government to smart grids.
  • Creating jobs in tech, engineering, systems integration, and operations.
  • Keeping African data in Africa, and using it to improve African lives.

Ghana is already showing what this future can look like. With partners like Onix providing the foundational infrastructure, we are not just imagining smart cities—we are building them.

Final Word: It Starts with the Infrastructure

Smart traffic lights. Telemedicine. e-Agriculture. e-Learning. These are not isolated innovations—they are part of an ecosystem. One that depends on high-performance, resilient, secure data infrastructure.

Is your business ready to build the future? Join Onix in powering Ghana’s smart transformation—from the ground up.

CONTACT US NOW!

item.title: Not Just a Panel: A Blueprint for Digital Africa at GITEX AFRICA 2025
item.dc:creator: Samuel
item.content:encoded:
At GITEX AFRICA 2025, Onix Data Centre had the privilege of contributing to one of the event’s most critical conversations: The Future of Green Computational Power in Africa. Represented by CEO Razak Awudulai on a high-impact panel, and joined at the event by CFO Samuel Osew-Kwatia, Onix was proud to engage in the discussions shaping Africa’s digital trajectory.

Why This Panel Mattered

Titled around sustainable infrastructure and digitisation, the panel tackled more than just data centres—it questioned how Africa can lead rather than follow in the global tech race. Razak brought a practical, policy-aware perspective to the conversation, urging leaders and institutions to treat energy, technology, and governance as a single, integrated ecosystem.

Here’s what stood out from the discussion:

1. Power and Technology Can’t Be Regulated Separately

Razak drew attention to a core challenge many African countries face: energy and ICT policy fall under different ministries. This often leads to fragmented regulation and slow progress. He argued for a top-down regulatory approach, where governments look at infrastructure holistically—setting unified policies that support data centres, fibre providers, and the broader tech ecosystem in tandem.

“If power policy sits in one ministry, and tech in another, we’re designing systems in isolation. We need synergy, not silos.” — Razak Awudulai

This is especially critical as the region sees an influx of data infrastructure projects. Without harmonised planning, issues like energy pricing, import tariffs on ICT equipment, and land use policy can collide, delaying or derailing major investments. Razak’s point is a reminder that regulation, when aligned, can be a growth enabler—but when disjointed, it becomes a bottleneck.

2. National Advantage Must Shape Energy Strategy

Different countries must embrace the energy sources they are uniquely equipped to harness. Ethiopia was cited as a successful example of leveraging hydropower to attract data-focused investments. Similarly, Razak suggested that nations like Nigeria could make the most of natural gas as a transitional clean energy source, especially if governments offer the right incentives.

In this framing, sustainability isn’t just about choosing the greenest solution—it’s about choosing the most viable and scalable one. Countries that understand their comparative advantage in energy can build reliable foundations for tech investment. But this also requires clear planning and proactive dialogue between government and private sector players.

3. Green Infrastructure Needs Green Finance

Razak pointed out the financial hurdles of deploying sustainable infrastructure—from solar power to energy-efficient equipment. He advocated for tax relief, import duty reforms, and smart subsidies that would encourage the private sector to invest in long-term sustainability. Without this support, the capex requirements can be prohibitive, especially for new entrants.

Beyond the initial cost, financing models must evolve to reflect the long-term economic and environmental return of green infrastructure. Power purchase agreements (PPAs), climate-linked financing instruments, and blended public-private models could all play a role. Governments, investors, and operators alike need to rethink how we value and support the backbone of the digital economy.

4. AI Must Speak to African Problems

Perhaps the most forward-looking insight came as Razak questioned the rush to implement AI tools in African data centres.

“Are we solving our own problems—or just hosting someone else’s algorithms?”

He called for investment in local research and development, so that Africa’s data centres not only support the global cloud economy but also power homegrown solutions tailored to the continent’s unique needs.

This raises important questions about data sovereignty, language inclusion, and what kinds of innovation we choose to prioritise. From agricultural AI models in local dialects to fintech algorithms tuned to informal economies, the opportunity is vast—but only if we invest in building AI ecosystems that reflect the reality on the ground.

A Moment of Momentum

Joining Razak at GITEX was Onix CFO Samuel Osew-Kwatia, who described the event as “a meaningful convergence of people building real, scalable impact in Africa.” He highlighted the value of GITEX AFRICA not just as a stage for insight, but as a space for partnerships and possibility.

For Onix, the event confirmed what we already believe: Africa has the potential not only to host the digital future, but to design it on its own terms.

item.title: LINX Accra at Onix: Building Ghana’s Internet Exchange Point at a Tier IV Data Centre
item.dc:creator: Samuel
item.content:encoded:
Last week marked an exciting milestone for Onix Data Centres as we deepened our collaboration with the London Internet Exchange (LINX) through two impactful events in Accra, Ghana.

A Visit to the Facility: Building Interconnection from the Ground Up

On Tuesday, we had the pleasure of welcoming the LINX team to our flagship Tier IV-certified, carrier-neutral data centre on the outskirts of Accra. The visit brought together teams from Onix and Spectrum Fibre for an engaging and informative session focused on the future of LINX Accra, Ghana’s next Internet Exchange Point.

We were privileged to hear from Nurani Nimpuno, Joe Jefford, and Patrick Mbogo, whose presentations delivered not only technical clarity but a shared sense of ambition and purpose. Their insights helped us all understand what LINX Accra will bring to Ghana: faster interconnection, reduced latency, and a stronger digital infrastructure rooted in Africa.

As Ghana’s only Tier IV-certified facility, our data centre is built to provide the resilience, security, and flexibility needed to support an Internet Exchange Point of global standards. Onix’s strategic location, robust infrastructure, and carrier-neutral design make it the perfect environment to support a thriving interconnection hub. Having LINX connect directly within our facility will make it easier for networks to peer, exchange traffic locally, and dramatically improve performance across West Africa.

The official launch of LINX Accra is just around the corner. Watch this space for the announcement!

Information and Networking at Mokas: Strengthening Ghana’s Digital Ecosystem

To continue the conversation, we co-hosted an information and networking session with our partners at Mokas. This was an opportunity to bring together key players from the telecoms and internet ecosystem network operators, ISPs, enterprise providers and connectivity champions to explore what LINX Accra means in practice.

Over food, drinks, and vibrant conversation, the LINX team shared how a single cross-connect at Onix can unlock new opportunities for networks in Ghana and beyond. It was a practical, down-to-earth session that helped cement shared understanding and enthusiasm for what we are building together.

We are grateful to everyone who joined us at Mokas and made the evening such a success.

Looking Ahead: A New Era for Interconnection in Ghana

As we move closer to the official launch of LINX Accra, the enthusiasm and momentum behind this partnership continue to grow. Onix is proud to be the home of LINX in Ghana, and we remain committed to providing world-class infrastructure, carrier-neutral flexibility, and unmatched reliability.

Thank you once again to the LINX team for visiting, for your openness, and for the knowledge you shared with all of us. This is only the beginning.

Interested in how the LINX and Onix partnership could benefit your business? Get in touch with our team today to find out more.

item.title: Carrier-Neutral Data Centres: The Digital Freedom Africa Can’t Afford to Ignore
item.dc:creator: Samuel
item.content:encoded:
As Africa’s digital economy accelerates, the conversation around data centre connectivity and digital infrastructure is shifting. More organisations are scrutinising the fine print of their digital infrastructure-and one critical feature stands out for its strategic value: carrier neutrality.

What Is Carrier Neutrality in Data Centres and Why It Matters for Africa

Carrier neutrality refers to a data centre’s ability to offer clients access to multiple internet service providers (ISPs) and telecom carriers. It is a defining feature of modern, high-performance colocation services in Ghana and beyond. Unlike facilities that tie clients to a single network provider, carrier-neutral data centres operate as open platforms, empowering clients to choose the best providers for their needs.

This flexibility becomes especially vital in emerging digital markets where infrastructure is still evolving, pricing is variable, and access to stable, high-performance connectivity can make or break business operations.

Freedom of Choice = Strategic Flexibility

Carrier-neutral environments allow businesses to avoid vendor lock-in, mix and match connectivity providers, and design customised network strategies. Whether optimising for speed, cost, security, or redundancy, clients benefit from the freedom to make decisions that serve their long-term goals, not the limitations of a single provider’s infrastructure.

Redundancy That Delivers Business Continuity

True redundancy means more than just having backup power. It includes being able to reroute data through alternative networks if a provider goes down. Multi-carrier options provide real resilience, essential for sectors where downtime has high costs, such as banking, healthcare, and e-commerce.

Lower Costs, Improved Performance

Carrier neutrality fosters competition within the data centre, which can reduce costs and improve service levels. Businesses can negotiate better rates, achieve lower latency, and tap into more efficient bandwidth options. In five years, your business will need more bandwidth, lower latency, and seamless multi-cloud access. The question is, will your infrastructure be ready, or will it hold you back?. This is especially important across West Africa, where international bandwidth pricing and network diversity are still evolving.

Carrier Neutral Colocation: Scalability and Speed to Market

A key advantage of carrier-neutral colocation data centres is how quickly clients can onboard or switch providers, deploy hybrid cloud strategies, and integrate new digital services. Your competitors are already looking for ways to cut telecom costs and scale faster. Are you?. For enterprises scaling across borders or launching new platforms, the ability to spin up or migrate workloads with minimal delay is invaluable.

Cloud Integration and Global Reach

Carrier neutrality is also essential for businesses integrating with global cloud platforms. A neutral facility typically supports on-ramps to major public cloud providers, as well as interconnections with SaaS ecosystems and international IXPs. This enables low-latency access to the global internet and cloud infrastructure.

Supporting Regional Connectivity Goals

As African nations prioritise digital transformation and data sovereignty, carrier-neutral data centres play a central role. By acting as open interconnection hubs, they attract multiple ISPs and carriers, reduce reliance on international transit routes, and support the development of local digital ecosystems.

Onix operates a Tier IV-certified, carrier-neutral facility just outside Accra. With access to many network providers, including Tier I carriers and satellite services, Onix enables businesses to thrive in a highly flexible and reliable environment. By putting customer choice and ecosystem resilience first, this facility plays a critical role in positioning Ghana as a digital leader in the region. Yet, too many companies still choose convenience over control, locking themselves into rigid, single-carrier setups that cost more and deliver less. As Africa’s digital economy matures, businesses that fail to demand carrier neutrality risk falling behind in resilience, speed, and innovation.

Sustainability and Infrastructure Design

Beyond connectivity, the best carrier-neutral facilities are also embracing sustainable design. Solar energy, intelligent cooling systems, and water recycling are increasingly part of the picture-demonstrating that high-performance infrastructure can align with environmental goals.

Future-Proofing Africa’s Digital Infrastructure with Carrier Neutrality

Carrier neutrality is not just a technical feature. It’s a foundational principle for building resilient, agile, and future-ready digital infrastructure across Africa’s emerging markets. As more organisations across Africa embrace cloud services, digital payments, and data-driven innovation, the ability to control and customise their connectivity strategies will become non-negotiable.

For any business evaluating data centre options, carrier neutrality should be near the top of the checklist. It’s a quiet feature-with powerful implications. For more information please CONTACT US.
item.excerpt:encoded: Carrier-neutral data centres are reshaping Africa’s digital future—offering businesses the freedom to choose, the flexibility to grow, and the resilience to thrive. Learn how this invisible feature delivers real-world impact for companies across the continent.

item.title: Data Centres vs. Decarbonisation: Can Africa Have Both?
item.dc:creator: Samuel
item.content:encoded:
The Global Race for Digital Infrastructure

Across Southeast Asia, countries like Malaysia, Indonesia, and the Philippines are in a digital infrastructure arms race, each vying to become the region’s next big data hub. But as the server racks multiply, so too does electricity demand. Malaysia alone is on track to multiply its data centre power use by almost eight times by 2030, a jump that would rival the entire electricity consumption of Singapore.

The result is a dilemma. Either countries rapidly invest in clean energy or risk letting their digital future become powered by coal and diesel. Without urgent action, the very infrastructure meant to enable the future will drag economies back into fossil dependence. This is the uncomfortable truth: digital transformation, without energy transformation, can become a climate liability.

A Wake-Up Call for Africa

This is not a distant problem for Africa. It is a window into what is about to happen here.

Africa's digital rise is underway. Cloud adoption is surging. Content demand is localising. Fintech, AI, and enterprise software are scaling. Governments are digitising services, banks are moving to the cloud, and startups are emerging daily with data-hungry applications. All this requires a physical backbone: data centres.

But data centres are not just buildings with servers. They are power-intensive ecosystems. They require constant electricity, advanced cooling, high connectivity, and guaranteed uptime. If not managed carefully, they can become some of the most carbon-intensive assets in a country.

What Southeast Asia Teaches Us

The lesson from Southeast Asia is clear. Without proper planning, data centres can lock countries deeper into fossil dependency. Malaysia could see a sevenfold increase in emissions from data centres by 2030. Indonesia’s Java grid, where most of its facilities are located, is still coal-powered. The emissions risk is real.

Ghana’s Window of Opportunity

In Ghana, early examples are showing what’s possible. Some facilities, like Onix in Accra, are beginning to integrate solar energy to cover daytime usage, with plans to expand to full 24/7 clean power through battery systems. It is a step forward, but the broader question remains: will the rest of the region follow suit?

The stakes are high. Ghana's power grid is already stretched. In many parts of West Africa, electricity access is unreliable and prices are volatile. Much of the power still comes from thermal plants running on fossil fuels. If data demand continues to grow without serious energy planning, we will see the rise of generator-powered digital infrastructure – clean tech running on dirty fuel.

A Clean Energy Strategy for Data Centres

But with the right strategy, this challenge becomes an opportunity. Data centre development can drive investment in solar, wind, and smart grid infrastructure. It can force innovation in energy efficiency. It can catalyse energy market reform.

So what must be done?

Governments need to embed digital infrastructure into national energy strategies. That means creating policies that allow direct clean energy procurement for data centre operators, such as renewable energy certificates or power purchase agreements. It means setting energy efficiency standards that match global benchmarks. And it means rethinking where we build and how we power these facilities.

Regional planning is also critical. There is no reason why data centres should only exist in capital cities with fragile grids. With fibre connectivity expanding, they can be sited near renewable energy hubs and still serve national needs.

The Urgency of Planning Now

Ghana and other African countries now have a chance to lead. Not just in building digital infrastructure, but in showing how it can be clean, reliable, and resilient. A handful of pioneers are showing it is possible. But we need more. More ambition, more support, more alignment between the digital and energy agenda.

Because data centres are not a luxury. They are the engines of economic growth, innovation, and digital sovereignty. And if we are not careful, they will become engines of emissions too.

Africa can build a digital future. But whether that future is green or grey depends entirely on the choices made right now.

Africa’s digital future must be clean, resilient, and ready. If you’re a policymaker, investor, or enterprise with a stake in that future, we’d love to hear from you.

Get in touch and let’s shape the next phase together.
item.excerpt:encoded: Africa’s data centre boom is coming fast. Will it power a clean digital future, or lock us into fossil fuels? Ghana has a rare chance to lead.

item.title: Reflections from Sandton: Insights from the Pan African Data Centre Conference
item.dc:creator: onixdc
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this week, our team had the opportunity to join industry leaders and innovators in Sandton, Johannesburg, for the Pan African Data Centre Conference. The two-day event gathered experts from across the continent and beyond to explore the most pressing challenges, biggest opportunities, and transformative trends shaping Africa's digital infrastructure future.

Here are seven of the most compelling themes that emerged from the sessions we attended:

1. Data Centres as Engines of Economic Transformation

Data centres are no longer just facilities for storage and uptime. They are foundational to Africa's digital future, enabling cloud adoption, accelerating government digitisation, and transforming traditional sectors like mining, agriculture, and transport. More than infrastructure, they are becoming enablers of national competitiveness and industrial resilience. We saw examples of data-driven mining, smart agricultural models, and decentralised infrastructure hubs that are helping communities leap into the digital age.

Their role extends into the heart of Africa’s development priorities. With sovereign data strategies gaining momentum, the power to process, store, and analyse data locally is now being recognised as a core economic advantage. The message was loud and clear: control your data, control your future. For countries seeking both digital sovereignty and inclusive growth, investment in data centres is no longer optional. It's essential.

2. AI is Changing Everything, Including the Workforce

The AI revolution is reshaping how data centres are operated, staffed, and integrated into wider society. From recruitment to operations, AI tools like ChatGPT are now streamlining processes, boosting efficiency, and transforming how tasks are completed. We heard how workloads that once took days can now be tackled in under an hour. It's a dramatic shift in productivity that is rewriting job descriptions and expectations across the industry.

But with great innovation comes a crucial warning: those who do not adapt risk being left behind. AI will not replace every job, but it will replace every job that doesn’t evolve. This is where Africa’s youth come in. With the youngest population globally, digitally native and eager to learn, there is enormous opportunity. The conference called for urgent investment in AI training, coding education, gender-inclusive programmes, and new learning models that go beyond traditional universities. Africa can lead, but only if it prepares its people now.

3. Adapting Global Standards to Local Realities

In a sector where global benchmarks are often copied and pasted, one project stood out. An initiative funded by the European Commission is helping African data centres adopt and adapt Europe’s energy efficiency Code of Conduct. This isn’t about importing rigid frameworks. It’s about tailoring world-class methods to suit African infrastructure, climate, and operational contexts. That means training, phased implementation, and peer-driven improvement.

The initiative was one of the most practical and forward-thinking discussed at the conference. Operators will benefit from structured guidance, transparency, and a framework for continuous progress. At Onix, we are especially excited about this direction. With our investment in solar generation and our long-term plans to move fully off-grid, we are in a strong position to meet many of these requirements from the outset. This aligns directly with our sustainability vision and our commitment to lead the industry not only in capacity, but in responsibility.

4. Talent is the Sector’s Greatest Challenge and Opportunity

No matter how advanced the technology, it's the people who keep data centres running. Right now, the human capital gap is one of the industry's greatest risks. Sessions highlighted the brain drain of skilled African professionals, many of whom are leaving for opportunities in Europe, North America, and Asia. Nearly 40 percent of participants cited retention as a critical issue. It’s not just about training more people. It’s about building an ecosystem where they want to stay.

The conversation around HR and workforce development was refreshingly honest. While technical upskilling is vital, it must be matched with improved quality of life, competitive salaries, and a culture of respect and belonging. HR leaders were called to the table alongside engineers, recognising that organisational culture, career growth, and community engagement are just as important as rack density and cooling technology. Africa’s digital future depends on its ability to nurture and keep talent at home.

5. Supply Chain and Procurement Bottlenecks Are Holding Back Progress

If Africa's data centre sector is a fast-moving train, its supply chain is the section of track most in need of repair. Delegates spoke of long delays for spare parts, inflexible procurement frameworks, and tariffs as high as 25 percent that make components prohibitively expensive. Global suppliers often prioritise larger, Western hyperscale projects, leaving African operators scrambling to catch up.

The effects are systemic. Delays reduce uptime, inflate project timelines, and undermine investor confidence. Some operators are turning to innovative workarounds like local battery filling to extend shelf life in unreliable grid environments. But the call was clear. It’s time for African governments, vendors, and industry associations to come together to streamline procurement, reduce trade barriers, and strengthen regional manufacturing. Resilience isn’t built on power systems alone. It must include reliable, regional supply chains.

6. Operational Culture Needs to Catch Up with Design Standards

The technology is evolving, but is the culture? While billions are spent designing Tier III and Tier IV facilities, less attention is given to what happens after launch. Over 70 percent of outages are caused by human error, and 52 percent of staff don’t consistently follow operational procedures. The gap between build and run is costing the industry more than we admit.

However, change is underway. New tools, from DCIM platforms to commissioning apps, are helping teams enforce quality, monitor environments, and make data-driven decisions. Cultural transformation is harder to engineer than server rooms, but it’s just as vital. As AI, high-density workloads, and hybrid architectures become the norm, operators must embrace a mindset of discipline, training, and transparency. The future of uptime depends on it.

7. Africa's Digital Future Must Be Inclusive, Sovereign and Strategic

The conference closed on a visionary note. Africa must build its own digital backbone, on its own terms. That means embracing sovereignty, owning the infrastructure, setting the policies, and shaping the content. But it also means strategy. We need to invest wisely, regulate smartly, and include everyone, especially the underserved and the landlocked.

The rise of sovereign AI, Africa-focused cloud platforms, and culturally rooted digital experiences offers a new path forward. The idea that Africa can shape the next wave of digital creativity is no longer far-fetched. It’s already happening. The question is whether we will seize it. The call from Sandton was for collaboration, courage, and clarity. And for those of us committed to building this future, the time to act is now.

In Closing

As Africa’s demand for compute, storage, and connectivity continues to grow, the conversation is evolving. It's no longer just about uptime or latency. It's about people, policy, energy, sovereignty, and the systems that tie them together.

At Onix, we return from this conference more determined than ever to play a meaningful role in this journey. We thank the organisers for a deeply insightful and collaborative event, and we look forward to building the future of Africa’s digital backbone together.

If you want to learn more about Onix and how we are pushing the boundaries of data centres in Africa, please get in contact!
item.excerpt:encoded: From AI-driven operations to data sovereignty, this year’s Pan African Data Centre Conference brought together the big ideas shaping Africa’s digital infrastructure. Onix joined industry leaders in Sandton to explore how we can build smarter, greener, and more inclusive data centres, and why our off-grid ambitions put us ahead of the curve.

item.title: LINX Accra Launches: A New Era for Local Interconnection in Ghana
item.dc:creator: onixdc
item.content:encoded:
On Thursday 3 July 2025, Ghana marked a major milestone in its digital development with the official launch of LINX Accra, a new Internet Exchange Point (IXP) that will serve both Ghana and the wider West African region.

See below for all the photos

The launch of LINX Accra represents the first time the globally respected London Internet Exchange (LINX) has established a physical presence in West Africa. By enabling direct local exchange of internet traffic, it is expected to significantly improve the quality and resilience of digital services throughout the country.

Speaking at the evening launch event, held at Sandbox Beach Club in Accra, the Minister for Communications, Digital Technology and Innovation, Honourable Samuel Nartey George (MP), welcomed the LINX team on behalf of President John Dramani Mahama and the people of Ghana. He described Ghana as a gateway to Africa and praised the LINX initiative as aligning with the government’s broader goal to improve internet access, affordability and user experience.

“This development is a huge step toward improving customer experience,” the Minister said. “Having an Internet Exchange Point right here in Ghana means we do not have to transmit traffic all the way to Europe before it gets back to our phones. That reduces latency, improves speed, and ensures a much better experience for users.”

He also emphasised the importance of collaboration in building the country’s digital ecosystem.

“We are not in competition. This industry thrives on cooperation,” he noted. “I am pleased to see the synergy between LINX and local data centres. This is the kind of digital unity that drives national development.”

The Minister was introduced by Onix CEO Razak Awudulai and was joined at the event by LINX CEO Jennifer Holmes, Head of Global Engagement Nurani Nimpuno, Head of Marketing Lynsey Buckingham, and Business Development Expert for Africa Patrick Mbogo. Also in attendance was Professor Nii Narku Quaynor, Chair of the Internet Society Ghana Chapter and a pioneer of internet development across Africa.

Jennifer Holmes highlighted the significance of LINX Accra within LINX’s global operations. She explained that the new IXP would support faster, more direct data flows between networks and content providers.

“With LINX Accra now operational, international content providers can localise their services in Ghana,” she said. “This will lead to faster streaming, quicker downloads and reduced traffic bottlenecks. Internet Service Providers will be able to connect directly to these centres, enhancing performance and reliability for consumers.”

The earlier part of the day saw a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the Onix Data Centres facility in Accra, where the LINX infrastructure is hosted alongside PAIX and Digital Realty. Onix CEO Razak Awudulai and CFO Samuel Osew Kwatia formally welcomed the LINX team and marked the official activation of the platform. The ceremony was a reflection of the growing collaboration between global and local partners in the development of internet infrastructure in Ghana.

LINX Accra is expected to bring immediate technical benefits by keeping local traffic within the country. This significantly reduces latency, lowers operational costs for network operators, and improves the delivery of services such as streaming, cloud applications, digital payments, and remote learning.

The initiative also opens up new opportunities for local content providers, developers and businesses to deliver services with greater efficiency and reach. For Ghana’s growing creative economy, gaming community, and startup ecosystem, access to a high-performance local exchange point creates the conditions needed for growth, innovation and global competitiveness.

As a Tier IV certified, carrier-neutral facility, Onix provides a robust and secure environment for an exchange point of this scale. With access to over 30 local and international network providers and a commitment to high-availability infrastructure, the Onix facility is a key part of the technical backbone supporting LINX Accra.

The collaboration between Onix, PAIX, and Digital Realty demonstrates a shared commitment to building digital infrastructure that serves the wider needs of the country. The partnership reinforces the idea that connectivity is not just about speed or uptime, but about inclusion, opportunity and national development.

At Onix, we are proud to be part of this milestone. LINX Accra is more than an infrastructure project, it is an investment in the digital future of Ghana. We thank the Ministry of Communications, LINX, the Internet Society Ghana Chapter, and our fellow data centre partners for their trust and collaboration.

Together, we are building the infrastructure that will carry Ghana into its next chapter as a regional leader in digital services. Get in contact with us at Onix for further information on how LINX Accra can support your business.

item.title: Inside the Engine Room: GCTU Students Explore Onix Data Centre
item.dc:creator: onixdc
item.content:encoded:
What the next generation of engineers had to say after visiting Ghana’s Tier IV facility

As Ghana’s digital economy grows, the people who will maintain and secure it need real-world exposure to the infrastructure that makes it possible.

Supporting the Engineers of Tomorrow

At Onix, we do more than build digital infrastructure. We believe in opening it up to those who will run it in the future.

As part of our commitment to support the next generation of engineers, we have been welcoming students from Ghana Communication Technology University for guided tours of our Tier IV data centre. These visits offer a real-world look into the systems and standards that sit behind the digital services they study in the classroom. From power and cooling to security and uptime, students are able to see how theory meets practice.

This is our way of giving back to the sector we are proud to be part of. It is a chance to answer their questions, encourage their ambitions, and show them what it really takes to operate a world-class data facility.

We are grateful to be part of their learning journey, and the visit gave us the opportunity to hear directly from the students about what they took away from the experience. What follows is a collection of their reflections and impressions, offering a detailed and personal look at how the tour connected with their learning and aspirations.

Kobina Ampiah, a Computer Science student, described the visit to our Tier IV-certified facility as "incredibly exciting and educational."

Kobina shared his key takeaways, which reflected the real-world application of his academic studies: from understanding how our 2N+1 design ensures 99.995 percent uptime, to seeing the robustness of our solar-powered infrastructure, supported by grid and generator backups. He also noted how our advanced cooling systems, reverse-osmosis water treatment, and biometric security connected classroom theory with practical cloud and data centre operations.

"Seeing this infrastructure up close," he wrote, "linked what we have learned in class to real-world cloud and data centre operations. It was a priceless learning experience."

One participant reflected on the broader value of the visit, noting it as an opportunity to gain firsthand insight into the practical operations of a modern Tier IV data centre and what it truly takes to run one successfully. The tour offered not just technical exposure but inspiration, and it stayed with them well before they even stepped inside the building.

Prince Lassey recalled first seeing the building from the outside, mistaking it for a private property due to its quiet exterior and solar panels. "What I found inside was a fortress for Ghana’s digital assets."

The tour was packed with insight. Students experienced eight layers of physical security, including fingerprint scanners, mantrap booths, and 24/7 surveillance. They saw how our redundant power systems, including more than 2,200 solar panels and multiple generators, are backed by dedicated UPS systems. They also learned about cold aisle containment, real-time monitoring, and our compliance with ISO 27001, ISO 9001, PCI-DSS, and Ghana’s Data Protection Act.

One student noted, "Security is not just a feature. It is a full system," a sentiment that reflected how thoroughly the tour demonstrated the integration of physical and digital protections across the facility.

Robert Akati wrote: "What does 99.995 percent uptime really look like? My classmates and I from GCTU recently got the rare opportunity to find out. From the mantrap with bulletproof glass to the dust-sensitive zones, we were inside the engine room of digital resilience."

Richard Nuhu also reflected on the experience as both enlightening and inspiring. He highlighted several key technical insights, including the facility's 99.995 percent uptime, its eight layers of physical protection, redundant systems with solar and backup generators, fireproofing measures, and long-term CCTV retention. He was particularly impressed by the Red, Blue, and Green Rooms, as well as the dedicated Meet Me Room for clients and ISPs. For him, the visit reinforced the idea that the cloud is not an abstract concept but something local and tangible, built on the ground by expert engineers.

Jael Amoo, a cybersecurity student, shared how the visit challenged and deepened her understanding of infrastructure security. "I thought I understood infrastructure security, but seeing it in person was something else entirely," she wrote. She described the facility’s 99.995 percent uptime and detailed the eight-layer security setup, including mantrap systems, biometric scanners, motion sensors, and constant surveillance. "What struck me most was how physical and digital security aren't separate things here, they're completely integrated." Her reflections captured the critical insight that in a facility like Onix, every system plays a part in safeguarding digital operations.

Elisha Maxwell Hutchinson also shared a thoughtful summary of the visit. As a cybersecurity student, he was particularly interested in the facility’s resilience and network design. He highlighted the integration of redundant power systems, cold-aisle containment, early fire detection technologies, and intrusion detection systems. Elisha noted the importance of carrier-neutral peering and global interconnectivity, especially through LINX Accra and Angola Cables. For him, the tour reinforced key ideas around zero-trust environments, cloud-native architecture, and hybrid network design. His perspective reflected a strong awareness of how physical, network, and governance layers work together to protect critical infrastructure at scale.

Sarkodie Dennis, passionate about network engineering and digital infrastructure, described the visit as a deep dive into Ghana’s digital core. He focused on ONIX as a benchmark for next-generation data centre design in West Africa. His highlights included multi-homed connectivity through Angola Cables, 2N redundant power systems, CRAC units for precision cooling, intelligent PDUs, and a 726kWp solar array supporting renewable energy goals. For him, the facility is more than just a location. It is the digital backbone supporting Ghana’s cloud economy, financial services, content delivery, and emerging AI applications. The experience reinforced his belief that Africa’s digital future is already here, and that it is being engineered with intent and precision.

Nathan Dankwa, also passionate about networking and infrastructure, described the visit to ONIX as both insightful and inspiring. He was struck by the facility’s commitment to both reliability and sustainability. He pointed to the Tier IV certification, 2N redundant power systems, and Angola Cables ecosystem as clear signs of ONIX's role in Ghana’s digital evolution. He also highlighted the centre’s use of a 640kWp solar farm as an example of responsible engineering, blending environmental awareness with high-performance design. In his words, ONIX is not just a data centre, it is the heart of Ghana’s growing digital economy.

Arimiyahu Ibrahim described the visit as a once-in-a-lifetime chance to see inside a Tier IV data centre. He reflected on the many layers of technical and physical safeguards, including 99.995 percent uptime, biometric scanning, bulletproof glass, and dedicated UPS systems. He was struck by the facility’s scale, its certifications, and the clarity with which security and uptime are designed into every layer. "Security isn’t just a feature, it’s a full system," he wrote. For Arimiyahu, the visit offered more than just a lesson in infrastructure. It was a reminder that the cloud is local, built and managed by expert engineers working behind the scenes in facilities like Onix.

And there were lighter moments too. "I even got a bar of chocolate for correctly answering a question during the tour," Emmanuel Nii Okai wrote. "The answer? Where else does Onix operate outside Ghana? Senegal."

One comment summed up the tone shared by many. "Truly a once-in-a-lifetime experience that fuels my passion for cloud innovation in Africa."

We would like to sincerely thank all the students who took the time to reflect on their visit and share their thoughts with us, including Roland Daniels, Emmanuel Nii Okai, Herbert Seshie, Robert Akati, Easteric Empeh, Kofi Eyaa Ainuson, Prince N, Joseph Mompi, Kobina Ampiah, Richard Nuhu, Jael Amoo, Elisha Maxwell Hutchinson, Sarkodie Dennis, Nathan Dankwa, Arimiyahu Ibrahim, and others we may have missed.

We look forward to welcoming more future engineers and sharing what it takes to power the digital economy securely, sustainably, and proudly from Ghana. If you are interested to learn more about Ghana's digital infrastructure, reach out to us!
item.excerpt:encoded: As part of our ongoing commitment to support future engineers, Onix recently welcomed students from Ghana Communication Technology University (GCTU) for a guided tour of our Tier IV-certified facility. The visit offered a rare look behind the scenes of Ghana’s most advanced data centre, giving students real-world exposure to the systems that power our digital economy. From redundancy and security to sustainability and network infrastructure, their reflections revealed not only what they learned, but why it mattered.

item.title: Why Ghana Is Emerging as Africa’s Next Data Centre Powerhouse
item.dc:creator: onixdc
item.content:encoded:
Africa’s digital infrastructure is undergoing rapid transformation. While South Africa, Nigeria, Egypt, Morocco and Kenya have traditionally dominated the data centre conversation, a new group of countries is stepping into the spotlight. Ghana is chief among them.

According to new insights from DC Byte, Ghana is now West Africa’s largest retail colocation hub by total IT capacity. Though live capacity remains modest today, the market is expected to grow tenfold in the coming years. Analysts already consider it a strong candidate for Africa’s next major hyperscale destination.

This growth is not an isolated development. It reflects a broader shift in the African data centre map. Capacity is no longer concentrated in a few core hubs. As DC Byte notes, North and West Africa now account for the second and third largest shares of tracked capacity across the continent. Ghana’s emergence marks a decentralisation of Africa’s digital backbone and a strategic pivot toward distributed infrastructure.

Ghana’s rise is being driven by three key factors:

  • Connectivity and Strategic Positioning: The country is already served by multiple international submarine cables—including ACE, MainOne, GLO-1, WACS and SAT-3—which position it as one of the best-connected nations in West Africa. Its substantial and ever expanding carrier presence, along with improving interconnection options, is transforming Ghana into a connectivity gateway for cloud and content providers seeking low-latency infrastructure close to end users.
  • Scalable, Sustainable Infrastructure: West Africa has over 440 MW of data centre capacity in the pipeline, and Ghana is set to take a significant share. Local operators are building at scale, combining technical resilience with green innovation. Facilities like Onix run entirely on solar power during the day, with battery systems planned to enable around-the-clock renewable operations. Smart water use, advanced cooling systems and waste recycling are helping to define new standards for environmentally responsible infrastructure on the continent.
  • Market Readiness and Real Demand: This growth is not speculative—it is already underway. Colocation racks are filling fast. Demand is coming from banks, fintechs, ISPs, public agencies and international firms seeking local presence in West Africa. The ecosystem is shifting from early-stage development to an active, maturing marketplace. Ghana is no longer preparing for the digital future—it is living it.

Africa’s Evolving Data Centre Landscape: Key Trends

Source: DC Byte – Africa Data Centres 2025

What This Means for the Industry

The momentum behind Ghana’s data centre sector sends a clear message to investors, hyperscale cloud players and regional enterprises alike: the infrastructure gap is closing, and first-movers are already reaping the benefits. For hyperscalers, this is a window to establish early dominance in a location with both local demand and strong onward connectivity. For African enterprises, it offers the chance to host data locally with higher resilience, lower latency and improved compliance.

For regulators and policymakers, Ghana’s emergence is a case study in the value of supporting open, carrier-neutral infrastructure and renewable energy adoption. It also reinforces the importance of aligning local regulation with the needs of an increasingly globalised digital economy.

Africa’s data centre map is changing. Ghana is not only part of that change. It is helping lead it.

To explore how your organisation can grow with Ghana’s digital infrastructure, get in touch with Onix

item.title: The Hidden Cost of Latency: Why Every Millisecond Matters in Ghana’s Digital Economy
item.dc:creator: onixdc
item.content:encoded:
When a mobile money transaction takes too long to process, most people do not blame latency. They blame the app. When a government platform times out before a form is submitted, they blame the institution. And when a customer abandons a cart on an e-commerce site because the payment gateway fails, it is not the overseas server they blame. It is the business.

In Ghana's increasingly digital economy, every delay is a risk. Latency has become the invisible factor that shapes user experience, business performance, and public trust. And while milliseconds might seem minor, they accumulate into lost revenue, missed opportunities, and frustrated users.

Latency is not just a tech problem. It is a business problem. A trust problem. A growth problem.

What is latency, and why does it matter? 

Latency is the time it takes for data to travel from a user’s device to the server and back. It is measured in milliseconds. The longer the distance and the more network stops in between, the higher the latency.

While fast internet speed is about how much data can move at once, latency is about how long it takes a single interaction to complete. And for most digital tools in Ghana, whether it is a banking app, a school portal, or a payment gateway, that tiny delay can make or break the experience.

Latency directly impacts user satisfaction. A study by Google showed that even a 100 millisecond delay in load time can reduce conversion rates by 7 percent. In real-world Ghanaian terms, this could be the difference between a customer completing a mobile money transfer or walking away in frustration.

Where latency is hurting Ghana’s digital services

  • Mobile payments: A few seconds of delay can cause failed transactions or duplicate charges. In an ecosystem where trust is everything, that delay drives users to abandon digital services.
  • Banking apps: Login timeouts and delayed data sync create doubt in system reliability.
  • E-learning and video conferencing: Buffering, delays, and broken connections degrade the experience for students, teachers, and professionals.
  • Public services: Government portals experience frequent timeouts and delays, especially during peak hours.
  • API-dependent services: Local fintech, insurance, and logistics apps often rely on overseas platforms, creating friction and failed processes when latency spikes.

The hidden business cost For digital platforms, performance is everything. Slow interactions lead to:

  • Higher user churn
  • Cart abandonment
  • Failed transactions
  • Poor reviews
  • Reduced trust in local innovation

Over time, latency contributes to a perception that Ghanaian digital products are unreliable. But often, the problem is not the product. It is where it is hosted.

In sectors like fintech, healthcare, logistics, and education, delays are more than a nuisance. They are business liabilities. A failed payment in an e-commerce app is not just a lost transaction. It might be a lost customer. A delayed medical record upload could mean a postponed diagnosis. For digital entrepreneurs and enterprises in Ghana, latency undermines the very trust and reliability their users depend on.

The role of overseas hosting and poor infrastructure 

Many Ghanaian businesses host their platforms in Europe or North America. Some use cloud providers without a local presence. This means every click, every API call, every video frame must travel thousands of kilometres and back. That distance introduces lag.

And if the local internet infrastructure is inconsistent, it makes the problem worse. Even the best-designed app cannot overcome the delay introduced by geography and infrastructure gaps.

High latency becomes even more problematic in moments of peak usage, such as payroll day, Black Friday sales, or student registrations. This is when the stakes are highest and when systems are most vulnerable. Overseas hosting may be affordable, but the real cost is hidden in broken transactions, failed logins, and user frustration.

Why local hosting changes everything 

Hosting data and services within Ghana dramatically reduces latency. It keeps data closer to users. It shortens the route. It means video calls connect faster, payments complete quicker, and APIs do not timeout.

This is where Onix Data Centre stands apart. As Ghana’s only Tier IV-certified, carrier-neutral data centre, Onix provides not just world-class uptime, but critical low-latency local infrastructure. With access to over 30 networks, multiple Tier I carriers, and cloud on-ramps, platforms hosted at Onix enjoy faster connections, lower risk of failure, and better user experience.

The advantages of local hosting are not only technical. They are strategic. Keeping data within borders also aligns with data sovereignty concerns and builds resilience against international disruptions. And it supports the broader goal of digital independence in Ghana and across West Africa.

Local infrastructure is local advantage 

n a competitive digital landscape, milliseconds matter. They determine whether a payment goes through, whether a customer completes a form, whether a meeting starts on time.

If your platform is slow, your users will not wait. They will walk away.

To grow Ghana's digital economy, we need to invest in infrastructure that reduces latency, improves reliability, and keeps data close to home. Because when we host locally, we compete globally.

Local infrastructure is no longer a backend decision. It is a business advantage.

Don’t let distance slow you down.

Host locally with Onix to give your users the speed, reliability and trust they deserve. Contact us here now!

item.title: Digital Africa Summit Ghana 2025: Charting the Future of AI and Infrastructure
item.dc:creator: onixdc
item.content:encoded:
On 3 September 2025, Accra hosted the inaugural Digital Africa Summit Ghana, a high-level gathering co-organised by the Government of Ghana and the GSMA. The event brought together policymakers, regulators, industry leaders, innovators, development partners and civil society to align on Ghana’s digital progress and the actions required to close gaps ahead of 2029.

Event Context and Highlights

  • The Government emphasised that technology is a sector of sectors, carrying agriculture, health, education, manufacturing, and finance on its back. Ghana’s goal is to accelerate digitalisation to transform productivity and improve lives across every domain.
  • The GSMA presented its national digitalisation report for Ghana, showing strong performance in mobile money and 4G coverage, but also a persistent 62% usage gap where covered citizens are not yet connected.
  • Recent reforms such as the removal of the e-levy, spectrum neutrality, and the expansion of rural fibre were identified as major steps forward.
  • By 2029, the right reforms could increase unique internet users by 43%, drive billions in GDP growth, and create hundreds of thousands of jobs.
The Panel: Powering Innovation – Data Centres as the Core of Africa’s AI Revolution

One of the standout sessions focused on the role of data centres in Africa’s AI-driven future. The panel brought together voices from finance, telecoms, academia, and infrastructure.

Representing Onix Dat a Centres and Broadspectrum, Kris M. Senanu joined the discussion to underline the strategic importance of world-class, carrier-neutral data centres for Ghana. His contributions emphasised:

  • Sovereignty and trust: Ghana’s most critical data should not leave the continent. Hosting it locally under Ghanaian law strengthens trust in fintech, govtech, and AI services.
  • Latency and reliability: AI, financial services, and health applications demand millisecond response times. With a Tier IV certified facility, Onix ensures 99.995% uptime and seamless low-latency interconnection.
  • Value capture: Keeping workloads in Ghana allows domestic SaaS, analytics, and AI services to flourish instead of exporting opportunity abroad.
  • Jobs and skills: Carrier-neutral, certified facilities create new pathways for Ghanaian engineers, operators, and cybersecurity professionals.
  • Investment climate: Certification, stable power agreements, and clear policy frameworks build confidence for investors and long-term partnerships.
Expected Outcomes if Implemented

The panel discussion outlined several expected outcomes if Ghana strengthens its data centre ecosystem:

  • Reduced latency and cost for fintech, healthtech, govtech, and AI workloads.
  • Growth of domestic digital services and innovation ecosystems.
  • Creation of technical jobs and training pipelines across ICT.
  • Greater investor confidence in Ghana’s digital economy.
Next Steps for Ghana’s Digital Infrastructure

The session also flagged actions to accelerate progress:

  • Establish a national data centre policy package covering residency, carrier neutrality, certifications, and interconnect standards.
  • Secure long-term, low-cost renewable and hybrid power agreements for facilities.
  • Expand in-country IXPs to end international hairpinning.
  • Build education-to-employment pathways for data centre skills.
  • Launch accelerators to drive local AI and data entrepreneurship.

The Digital Africa Summit Ghana 2025 reinforced that Ghana’s ambitions for digital leadership cannot be achieved without resilient infrastructure. As Kris Senanu made clear, Tier IV, carrier-neutral data centres like Onix, combined with Spectrum Fibre’s 7,500 km backbone, are not just support services, they are the backbone of Africa’s AI revolution.

For information about Onix Data Centres or Broadspectrum, and what we can do to empower your business locally in Ghana, get in contact!

item.title: Game On, Ghana: Why Local Infrastructure Is the Future of E-Gaming
item.dc:creator: onixdc
item.content:encoded:
End of a hard week. You and your friends across the world sit down to reignite your rivalries. Lobbies loaded. Call of Duty or FIFA, take your pick. The moment for glory comes. Final seconds. Enemy in your crosshairs. You pull the trigger. You jump in jubilation, only to see your opponents victorious. You slump back in a daze as your platoon roasts you through your headphones, echoing between your ears. “You are so bad. Just a simple shot.” But you know you did not miss. It was lag. The server was not in Accra. The distance made the difference. Your inputs took the long road and arrived too late.

What gamers experience when servers are hosted overseas

When Ghanaian players connect to servers in Europe or North America, packets travel thousands of kilometres. Even at the speed of light in fibre, distance adds delay. A practical rule of thumb is roughly 5 microseconds per kilometre in fibre (about 5 ms per 1,000 km one way). On a 5,000 km path, physics alone adds around 25 ms one way and ~50 ms round trip before you include routing, peering and queueing overheads. In real routes to Europe and North America, that budget climbs further. Put simply, every extra 1,000 km costs about 10 ms of round-trip time before routing and congestion. That delay turns up in aim duels, hit registration and movement. In fast shooters, extra latency measurably reduces performance in competitive play. In football titles, button presses feel like they hang. In battle royales, you lose trades you should win.

Ping, lag and matchmaking: why it matters

For competitive games, consistency is everything. High ping and jitter throw off aim timing and make shot registration feel unfair. Peeker's advantage becomes more pronounced. Matchmaking can struggle to form stable lobbies if the region pulls players to far-off servers. For creators, long round-trip paths to remote ingest servers increase dropped frames during busy evenings, hurting audience retention. As a rule of thumb, many players aim for sub-50 ms; penalties above ~100–150 ms become obvious. Consistency matters as much as raw ping, so watch jitter and packet loss. Hosting locally and peering directly help keep both ping and jitter low.

Why low-latency, local hosting unlocks better performance

Hosting game servers and related services in Ghana brings the action closer to players. Shorter paths reduce ping and jitter, improve hit registration, and make aim and movement feel responsive. It also helps matchmakers place Ghanaian players together more often, stabilising lobbies at peak times.

Two market shifts make local hosting in Ghana particularly attractive right now:

  1. New subsea capacity and resilience. Systems like Equiano and 2Africa are transforming international capacity to and from Africa, improving resilience and lowering latency to global platforms.
  2. Neutral peering in Accra. A public Internet exchange in Accra gives networks and platforms a place to peer locally, which reduces back-and-forth traffic to Europe and improves local traffic flows.
The opportunity for local esports, game dev and content creators

Lower latency and better peering change the equation for Ghana’s gaming ecosystem:

  • Esports. Tournament servers hosted locally cut ping variance, reduce lobby instability and allow broadcast teams to produce cleaner shows.
  • Game studios. Faster builds, asset sync and patch distribution improve team velocity. Local mirrors and CI/CD runners speed up daily work.
  • Creators. Stable upstreams and local peering with global platforms reduce buffering and dropped frames during live shows.

Across the continent, the games market is expanding quickly, driven by mobile and a surge of new players. As revenues rise, demand for reliable low-latency infrastructure follows.

Infrastructure building blocks for low-latency gaming in Ghana

For fast, fair online play, the infrastructure recipe is simple:

  • Proximity. Host game servers and ingest/relay nodes in Accra or as close to players as possible.
  • Neutral interconnection. Use a carrier-neutral data centre with a public Internet exchange so ISPs, platforms and CDNs can peer locally.
  • Redundant connectivity. Multiple carriers and diverse fibre routes to keep latency low and stable during faults.
  • Resilient power. UPS, generators and, where available, on-site solar to keep services online.
  • Edge services. Local caches, patch mirrors and CI/CD runners to speed updates and dev workflows.

Accra already has these building blocks in place through neutral facilities and a live Internet exchange. Onix is one of the providers delivering a Tier IV-certified, carrier-neutral environment that supports this model without locking anyone in.

What this means in practice

  • Lower ping for players. Servers in Accra remove thousands of kilometres of round-trip distance. Physics is on your side.
  • Smoother tournaments. Teams play on stable lobbies with fair hit registration and fewer disconnects.
  • Happier viewers. Local peering reduces the hop count to platforms, which cuts buffering during live streams.
  • Serious uptime. Tier IV design with 99.995 percent expected availability keeps brackets, streams and patch servers online.
Checklist to host locally in Ghana

  1. Pick a neutral home. Choose a carrier-neutral site in Accra with easy cross-connects and access to the public IXP.
  2. Connect smart. Peer locally, add cross-connects to multiple ISPs, and keep at least two diverse routes.
  3. Place the right workloads locally. Start with matchmakers and tournament servers, then add update mirrors, ingest/relay, VOD cache and build runners.
  4. Measure and iterate. A/B test ping, jitter and packet loss. Expand once the numbers prove out.
  5. Design for resilience. Confirm power, cooling and maintenance windows to protect events and leagues.

If you run an esports platform, studio or creator network in Ghana, pilot a local host. Coordinate with your ISP, community organisers and a neutral data-centre operator in Accra to spin up a small server or relay and measure the latency win. Contact us here to discuss further.

item.title: Ghana Asserts Digital Leadership at AFTS Accra 2025
item.dc:creator: onixdc
item.content:encoded:
Over three dynamic days in Accra, Ghana took centre stage at the Africa FinTech Summit 2025; not just as host, but as a driving force behind the continent’s digital future. Government officials, regulators, founders, investors and global tech players gathered at the Accra International Conference Centre to exchange bold ideas and build a collective path forward for fintech, AI, payments and data infrastructure in Africa.

The message was clear: Africa is no longer waiting for digital progress to arrive. It is building it, shaping it, and claiming ownership of the systems that will define its future.

Day 1: Policy, Strategy and a Call for Collaboration

The summit opened with a strong ministerial statement from Hon. Samuel Nartey George, Minister of Communications and Digital Technology, who urged African nations to work together on payment integration and digital sovereignty. His keynote underscored the urgency of building local infrastructure, harmonising data systems and ending reliance on foreign payment rails.

“AfCFTA remains a dream and a mirage if we do not make digital trade the centre pillar,” he said. “Let us put our egos aside and let PAPSS work.”

AI was a major theme across the event, beginning with Day 1 where Ghana’s nearly completed National AI Strategy was presented. Developed through close collaboration with academia and innovators, the strategy focuses on practical deployment in key sectors like agriculture, education and healthcare. Local language models and voice-first tools were highlighted as essential to overcoming barriers in literacy and access.

To support this, Ghana is finalising the Data Harmonisation Act, which will bring together key datasets from across government systems into a central AI-ready platform. Each ministry is expected to have AI use cases included in their KPIs from 2026 onwards.

The government also called on OpenAI and other global tech companies to support Ghana’s One Million Coders initiative, encouraging them to fund AI training for thousands of young people. These aren’t just pilot projects. They are nation-scale plans with timelines and accountability.

Day 2: Workshops, Builders and Action Plans

If Day 1 laid out the vision, Day 2 got practical. The programme included panel discussions, technical workshops and closed-door boardrooms. Infrastructure, policy design, capital access and creative finance models were all on the table.

Panel topics included:

  • Digital inclusion through infrastructure
  • Regulation and innovation
  • Pan-African payments (PAPSS)
  • Culture and finance
  • The gig economy and digital jobs
  • Startup funding and investor strategies

AI featured heavily throughout both days, with practical sessions on use cases, policy alignment and how to build safe, inclusive systems tailored for African needs. There was a consistent thread: AI can’t be a distant aspiration. It needs to solve real-world problems here and now.

Mike Ogbalu III, CEO of PAPSS, shared an update on progress: “We want Africans to be able to make payments to each other as easily as sending an SMS. Fund transfers are now settling in 7 seconds.”

He called on startups to think beyond borders. “You’ve built something that works in one country; come talk to us and let’s scale it to 54.”

Other voices echoed the spirit of collaboration:

“Your interests are not misaligned with policymakers. Be patient, open-minded and engage,” said Kwame Oppong from the Bank of Ghana.

“Fintech isn’t just about payments, it’s about building resilient economies,” added Olufunmi Fagbulu from VISA.

Larry Cooke from Binance delivered a sharp warning: “If African countries don’t find ourselves on the global blockchain ledger, foreign currencies will dominate local ends.”

Fintech Pitch Competition 

The day closed with a showcase of promising fintech innovators.

Pitch Competition

  • 1st Place: Yene Health – An Ethiopian femtech platform offering reproductive health tools such as period and pregnancy tracking, teleconsultations, e-pharmacy delivery and health content in local languages.
  • 2nd Place: Nyla Bank – A Shariah-compliant digital bank delivering ethical, multi-currency banking services with transparency, social responsibility and inclusive finance at its core.
  • 3rd Place: ProDetect – A Ghana-based AI-native fraud detection platform designed to protect African financial systems with real-time monitoring tailored to local transaction patterns.
Digital Infrastructure: More Than a Foundation

One message came through clearly across the event through Onix Data Centre discussions with stakeholders: fintech and AI can’t scale without serious infrastructure behind them. Stronger, faster and safer systems are not optional, they are essential. It’s not just about having a data centre. It’s about having facilities that are secure, efficient and sustainable enough to support the workloads of tomorrow.

As AI adoption grows, so does the demand for high-density computing, stable connectivity and climate-conscious power solutions. That’s why high-quality data centres must become a national priority, not an afterthought.

The Onix Perspective

At Onix, we see the shift happening already. Our Tier IV-certified data centre in Accra is designed to meet the demands that events like AFTS highlight. Real-time fintech transactions, national health systems, AI model training and more. With 100% solar coverage during the day and connectivity to over 30 networks, we provide the kind of environment needed to keep Africa’s digital ambitions moving forward.

We are proud to support this ecosystem, not just by housing data, but by helping power the platforms and services that make digital inclusion a reality.

Africa Is Not Waiting

AFTS Accra 2025 showed that Ghana is not waiting for the future to be delivered. It is building it through national strategies, policy frameworks, international partnerships and homegrown solutions. From AI and cross-border payments to infrastructure and innovation, the groundwork is being laid—boldly and visibly.

And as this ecosystem continues to grow, Onix will be right there, providing the space, speed and support that Africa’s digital future demands.

From a near-complete national AI strategy to a strong push for cross-border payment integration, the summit showcased how policy, innovation and infrastructure are coming together. With AI, fintech and digital trade dominating the agenda, one message rang clear: Africa’s future depends on strong, sustainable digital infrastructure.
